newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE - NZ election may bring tighter land purchase rules.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - NZ election may bring tighter land purchase rules.

text.p: Foreign buyers of New Zealand land, and in particular rural land, are likely to face much tighter restrictions after the October 12 election.

But despite the "economic nationalism" promoted by the opposition New Zealand First and Alliance parties there is unlikely to be a consensus to close the door on other forms of foreign investment if the conservative National Party is ousted.
The combined opposition is well ahead of the ruling National-United coalition in the opinion polls.

Under the newly-adopted German-style system of proportional representation, that should point to a change of government, but it is unclear whether the opposition will be able to form a single bloc to win the Treasury benches.
LAND A SPECIAL ISSUE FOR NEW ZEALANDERS, ESPECIALLY MAORIS

Foreigners have been steady but not spectacular buyers of New Zealand land, mainly for forestry and tourism ventures. But a combination of New Zealand's traditional reliance on farming and the special relationship that its Maori people claim with their "turangawaewae" (literally "place to stand") has made the issue an emotive one.
That was fuelled by the sale of cutting rights to 188,000 hectares (464,500 acres) of state forest on land claimed by Maoris, only two months out from the election.

New Zealand First and the left-wing Alliance have promised to buy back Forestry Corporation from a consortium of local companies Fletcher Challenge and Brierley Investments and Chinese investment company Citic.
The strongest line on foreign investment comes from New Zealand First, condemning what it calls the betrayal of selling state assets overseas and "flogging New Zealand off to the highest bidder".

It is rating about 20 percent in the polls but early in 1996 reached almost 30 percent after strong statements by leader Winston Peters about a loss of "economic control and sovereignty" and the high level of immigration.
Peters has since toned down his position, but would still limit foreign holdings to 25 percent in "key strategic assets" such as telecommunications, Air New Zealand Ltd, ports and other utilities.
He would not force the sale of holdings currently above that level. But when investors did come to sell, they would have to sell to New Zealanders.

Earlier this year Peters promised to ban land sales to foreigners, but has since limited the ban to rural land. Sources in his party told Reuters the policy required further work to iron out anomalies.

For instance, Peters has said big Australian fund managers such as AMP and National Mutual would be treated as foreign for the purposes of his policy. But that would cut across the Australian-New Zealand free trade and investment pact CER.

Peters is also campaigning for compulsory superannuation savings through either government or private schemes. Since saving would be funnelled into overseas-owned institutions which would be prevented from going above 24.9 percent in key assets, the two policies are potentially at odds.
LABOUR PARTY ALSO WANTS TIGHTER RULES ON LAND SALES
The opposition Labour Party, also polling around 20 percent, wants tighter rules on land sales.
Leader Helen Clark says land is "different". She said her personal view was that restricting foreign investment in general would be bad for the economy.

The left-wing Alliance, currently attracting about 12 percent support, has been a consistent critic of sales to foreigners. Its leader, Jim Anderton, left Labour during its last term in office after it sold Telecom New Zealand to Bell Atlantic and Ameritech.

The Alliance would ban rural land sales to non-residents and restrict commercial and industrial sales to companies with more than 49 percent foreign ownership. Restrictions would apply only to purchases of more than $10 million for residential property and $20 million for industrial land.
Tighter "national interest" criteria would apply, including environmental, investment, job creation, and employment equity considerations.

But despite the political heat in the issue Murray Horton, secretary of the major anti-foreign investment lobby group, the Campaign Against Foreign Control of Aotearoa (New Zealand), expects little change whatever the election outcome.

"With National we expect more of the same. Peters has done so many backflips on this issue, even if an opposition coalition won power there would only be a bit of tinkering rather than significant change," Horton said.
Under the current law, foreign investment is administered by the Overseas Investment Commission (OIC) under a regime which actively encourages equity in-flows.
Since 1990 foreign direct investment has grown by more than 100 percent, leaving New Zealand at March 1996 with a negative net investment position of some $73.3 billion.

The OIC tracks only approvals, not whether they are followed through (it last turned down an applications in 1990) but its latest report issued in August showed approvals for the 1995 year of $4.9 billion. Of that, $2.9 billion was new investment, with the balance made up transfers between overseas owners or changes involving no change in beneficial owner.

Approvals by value were dominated by New Zealand's traditional trading partners, with Australia ($1.4 billion) Britain ($1.1 billion) and the United States ($720 million) accounting for 67 percent of the total. Asian investors accounted for 18 percent.
The main areas of investment were forestry (29 percent) and manufacturing (nine percent).
The commission's powers over land purchases were tightened marginally in 1995, but in general the policy remains an open door.

In the six months to December 1995 the OIC granted consent to buy 41,775 hectares (103,200 acres) for $516 million, with 80 percent relating to forestry. In the past five years sales of land to foreigners amounted to 0.7 percent of New Zealand's land area but the trend has been upwards.
Since deregulation of financial markets in the 1980s both the New Zealand sharemarket and the bond market have become dominated by overseas cash.

Brokers Doyle Paterson Brown estimate 60.5 percent of the capitalisation of the NZSE-40 index is in foreign hands. Reserve Bank figures show 54.4 percent of all government securities are held by non-residents.
